LATAM
*chunk4*
```{r}
# Load the data frames from the RDS file
data_latam <- readRDS("Data/Input/updated_modern_dataset_climate_hill.rds") |>
  select(-c(mapr, mi, gdd0, mat, mtco, mtwa, alpha, age_bp))

data_latam

#Remover taxa con valores de cero
modern_pollen_latam <- data_latam |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -c(id_sample:entity_type),names_to = "taxa") |>
  filter(value > 0)

#Remover taxa que ocurren en menos del 1 % de las muestas
n_total <- n_distinct(modern_pollen_latam$id_sample)

aux1 <- modern_pollen_latam |>
  group_by(taxa) |>
  mutate(n_samples = n_distinct(id_sample)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(n_samples >= 0.002 * n_total) |>
  select(-n_samples)

#Funcion para manejar casos donde todos en el grupo son NAs
mode_na <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  if (length(x) == 0) {
    return(NA_character_)
  }
  names(sort(table(x), decreasing = TRUE))[1]
}

modern_pollen_latam <- aux1 |>
  group_by(id_sample) |>
  mutate(value = value / sum(value)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  arrange(taxa) |>
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols = c(id_sample:entity_type),
    names_from = "taxa",
    values_fill = 0
  ) |>
  select(-c(id_sample, entity_name)) |>
  group_by(latitude, longitude) |>
  summarise(
    across(
      where(is.numeric),
      ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)
    ),
    site_type = mode_na(site_type),
    entity_type = mode_na(entity_type),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(id_sample = paste0("ID_", row_number())) |>
  select(id_sample, everything())


modern_pollen_latam <- modern_pollen_latam |>
  select(id_sample:elevation, site_type, entity_type, everything()) |>
  select(-site_type, -entity_type)
  
modern_pollen_latam
```

```{r}
# 2. CRS métrico (para medir distancias) y resolución común
crs_metric <- "EPSG:6933"

# Comprobar
res(r_tcc_metric)

crs(r_tcc_metric)


#Convertir poligonos a terra

#land_eur_vect   <- vect(land_polyg_eur)
```

1. Preparar únicamente id_sample, latitud y longitud
*chunk16*
```{r}
# Puntos LATAM
pts_latam <- modern_pollen_latam |> dplyr::select(id_sample, latitude, longitude)
# Puntos Europa
pts_europa <- modern_pollen_europe |> dplyr::select(id_sample, latitude, longitude)

nrow(pts_latam)
nrow(pts_europa)
```

2. Trabajar en un CRS métrico

Como los radios son de 25 y 50 km, no quiero calcular distancias directamente en WGS84.
Para empezar, podemos utilizar una proyección métrica global. Una opción práctica para este análisis es EPSG:6933, que trabaja en metros y es apropiada para análisis espaciales globales.
*chunk17*
```{r}
pts_latam_vect <- vect(pts_latam, geom = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = "EPSG:4326")
pts_europa_vect <- vect(pts_europa, geom = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = "EPSG:4326")

crs_metric <- "EPSG:6933"
pts_latam_metric <- project(pts_latam_vect, crs_metric)
pts_europa_metric <- project(pts_europa_vect, crs_metric)

```

3. Extraer los píxeles dentro de 50 km
Aquí está una parte importante del diseño.
Vamos a crear buffers de 50,000 m alrededor de cada punto:
Y extraemos los píxeles del raster.
*chunk18*
```{r}
buffer50_latam <- buffer(pts_latam_metric, width = 50000)
buffer50_europa <- buffer(pts_europa_metric, width = 50000)


extract50_latam <- terra::extract(r_latam, buffer50_latam, cells = TRUE, xy = TRUE)
extract50_europa <- terra::extract(r_europa, buffer50_europa, cells = TRUE, xy = TRUE)

```


4. Añadir las coordenadas de cada punto
Necesitamos saber la distancia entre el centro de cada píxel y el punto correspondiente.
*chunk19*
```{r}
#Para LATAM:
coords_latam <- crds(pts_latam_metric)

coords_latam <- data.frame(point_id = seq_len(nrow(pts_latam_metric)),
                           point_x = coords_latam[, 1],
                           point_y = coords_latam[, 2])

#Para Europa
coords_europa <- crds(pts_europa_metric)

coords_europa <- data.frame(point_id = seq_len(nrow(pts_europa_metric)),
                            point_x = coords_europa[, 1],
                            point_y = coords_europa[, 2])


#Ahora podemos añadir esas coordenadas a las extracciones:
extract50_latam <- extract50_latam |> left_join(coords_latam, by = c("ID" = "point_id"))
extract50_europa <- extract50_europa |> left_join(coords_europa, by = c("ID" = "point_id"))
```


5. Calcular distancia de cada píxel al punto
Como estamos en metros:
*chunk20*
```{r}
extract50_latam <- extract50_latam |> mutate(distance_m = sqrt((x - point_x)^2 + (y - point_y)^2))

extract50_europa <- extract50_europa |> mutate(distance_m = sqrt((x - point_x)^2 + (y - point_y)^2))
```

```{r}
summary(extract50_europa$distance_m)
```

Ahora viene la parte de calcular los seis escenarios gaussianos. Como extract50_* son enormes, yo lo haría por región y por radio, evitando crear tres columnas permanentes de pesos.
Empezaría con LATAM y, cuando comprobemos que funciona, hacemos exactamente lo mismo para Europa.
Primero define los sigmas:
*chunk26*
```{r}
# Sigma para radio de 50 km
sigma50_100 <- 50000 / 100   # 500 m
sigma50_10  <- 50000 / 10    # 5,000 m
sigma50_3   <- 50000 / 3     # 16,666.67 m
sigma50_2   <- 50000 / 2     # 25,000 m

# Sigma para radio de 25 km
sigma25_100 <- 25000 / 100   # 250 m
sigma25_10  <- 25000 / 10    # 2,500 m
sigma25_3   <- 25000 / 3     # 8,333.33 m
sigma25_2   <- 25000 / 2     # 12,500 m
```


1. LATAM — escenarios de 50 km
Aquí usamos todos los píxeles de extract50_latam. La regla de NA será exactamente la que acordamos: si más de la mitad de los píxeles del buffer son NA, el resultado será NA.

GAUSSIAN-WEIGHTED TREE COVER WITHIN A 50-km RADIUS — LATIN AMERICA

Objective:
For each modern pollen sample (ID), calculate the mean tree cover within a circular 50-km radius, weighting each raster pixel according to its distance from the sampling point using a Gaussian function.

Pixels located close to the sampling point therefore contribute more strongly to the estimated tree-cover value than pixels located farther away.
Three Gaussian weighting scenarios are calculated using the SAME 50-km extraction radius but different sigma (σ) values:

* sigma = radius / 100 = 500 m
* sigma = radius / 10 = 5,000 m
* sigma = radius / 3 = 16,666.67 m

A smaller sigma produces a much stronger concentration of weight around the sampling point, whereas a larger sigma allows more distant pixels to contribute substantially to the final estimate.

Gaussian weighting function:
w = exp( - d² / (2 × σ²) )

where:
w = weight assigned to a raster pixel
d = distance between the centre of the raster pixel and the pollen sample
σ = standard deviation controlling the spatial decay of the Gaussian kernel

The Gaussian-weighted tree-cover estimate is:

TreeCover_weighted = Σ(tree_cover_i × w_i) / Σ(w_i)

Importantly, the denominator contains ONLY the weights associated with non-NA tree-cover pixels. Therefore, missing raster cells do not contribute either to the numerator or denominator.

Missing-data criterion:
# IMPORTANT:
     The NA criterion is evaluated within sigma, but the Gaussian weighted
     mean itself still uses all available pixels within the complete
     50-km extraction radius
--------------------------------------------------------
La mediana ponderada te dice el valor “central” de tree cover después de dar más importancia a los píxeles cercanos. El SD ponderado te dice cuánto varían los valores alrededor de esa media ponderada.

Además, ambos están en las mismas unidades que tree cover. Si tree cover está en %, entonces mediana y SD están en puntos porcentuales.

Mean weighted   = 70
Median weighted = 72
SD weighted     = 4

indicates a landscape concentrated around 70–72%, and therefore relatively homogeneous.

In contrast:
Mean weighted   = 70
Median weighted = 85
SD weighted     = 25

suggests a much more heterogeneous and possibly asymmetric landscape: many pixels have high cover values, but others have low values that pull the mean downward.

In fact, the combination of **mean + median + SD** is quite informative:

* `Mean ≈ Median` + low SD → relatively homogeneous landscape.
* `Mean ≈ Median` + high SD → substantial heterogeneity, but relatively symmetric.
* `Mean < Median` → low/extreme values are pulling the mean downward.
* `Mean > Median` → some high values are pulling the mean upward.
* large difference between mean and median + high SD → highly heterogeneous and asymmetric distribution.

What I **would not** do is directly interpret something like `SD = 15` versus `Median = 70` as a comparison of magnitude between the two metrics. The median represents **cover level**, whereas the SD represents **dispersion**.


*chunk27*
```{r}
results50_latam <- extract50_latam |>
  group_by(ID) |>
  summarise(
    # ========================================================================
    # SCENARIO 1
    # Radius = 50 km
    # sigma = 50 km / 10 = 5,000 m
    #
    # Missing-data rule:
    # Evaluate data availability only within one sigma (5 km).
    # If more than 50% of the pixels located within 5 km are NA,
    # the final estimate is assigned NA.
    #
    # The Gaussian-weighted statistics themselves use all valid pixels
    # within the complete 50-km extraction radius.
    # ========================================================================
    n_sigma10 = sum(distance_m <= sigma50_10),
    n_na_sigma10 = sum(is.na(tree_cover) & distance_m <= sigma50_10),
    # Gaussian-weighted mean
    Tree_Gaussian_50_sigma10 = if_else(n_sigma10 == 0 | n_na_sigma10 > n_sigma10 / 2, NA_real_, sum(tree_cover * exp(-(distance_m^2) / (2 * sigma50_10^2)), na.rm = TRUE) / sum(exp(-(distance_m[!is.na(tree_cover)]^2) / (2 * sigma50_10^2)))),
    # Gaussian-weighted standard deviation
    Tree_SD_50_sigma10 = if_else(n_sigma10 == 0 | n_na_sigma10 > n_sigma10 / 2, NA_real_, sqrt(sum(exp(-(distance_m^2) / (2 * sigma50_10^2)) * (tree_cover - Tree_Gaussian_50_sigma10)^2, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(exp(-(distance_m[!is.na(tree_cover)]^2) / (2 * sigma50_10^2))))),
    # Gaussian-weighted median
    Tree_Median_50_sigma10 = if_else(n_sigma10 == 0 | n_na_sigma10 > n_sigma10 / 2, NA_real_, matrixStats::weightedMedian(x = tree_cover[!is.na(tree_cover)], w = exp(-(distance_m[!is.na(tree_cover)]^2) / (2 * sigma50_10^2)))),
    # ========================================================================
    # SCENARIO 2
    # Radius = 50 km
    # sigma = 50 km / 3 = 16,666.67 m
    # ========================================================================
    n_sigma3 = sum(distance_m <= sigma50_3),
    n_na_sigma3 = sum(is.na(tree_cover) & distance_m <= sigma50_3),
    # Gaussian-weighted mean
    Tree_Gaussian_50_sigma3 = if_else(n_sigma3 == 0 | n_na_sigma3 > n_sigma3 / 2, NA_real_, sum(tree_cover * exp(-(distance_m^2) / (2 * sigma50_3^2)), na.rm = TRUE) / sum(exp(-(distance_m[!is.na(tree_cover)]^2) / (2 * sigma50_3^2)))),
    # Gaussian-weighted standard deviation
    Tree_SD_50_sigma3 = if_else(n_sigma3 == 0 | n_na_sigma3 > n_sigma3 / 2, NA_real_, sqrt(sum(exp(-(distance_m^2) / (2 * sigma50_3^2)) * (tree_cover - Tree_Gaussian_50_sigma3)^2, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(exp(-(distance_m[!is.na(tree_cover)]^2) / (2 * sigma50_3^2))))),
    # Gaussian-weighted median
    Tree_Median_50_sigma3 = if_else(n_sigma3 == 0 | n_na_sigma3 > n_sigma3 / 2, NA_real_, matrixStats::weightedMedian(x = tree_cover[!is.na(tree_cover)], w = exp(-(distance_m[!is.na(tree_cover)]^2) / (2 * sigma50_3^2)))),
    # ========================================================================
    # SCENARIO 3
    # Radius = 50 km
    # sigma = 50 km / 2 = 25,000 m
    # ========================================================================
    n_sigma2 = sum(distance_m <= sigma50_2),
    n_na_sigma2 = sum(is.na(tree_cover) & distance_m <= sigma50_2),
    # Gaussian-weighted mean
    Tree_Gaussian_50_sigma2 = if_else(n_sigma2 == 0 | n_na_sigma2 > n_sigma2 / 2, NA_real_, sum(tree_cover * exp(-(distance_m^2) / (2 * sigma50_2^2)), na.rm = TRUE) / sum(exp(-(distance_m[!is.na(tree_cover)]^2) / (2 * sigma50_2^2)))),
    # Gaussian-weighted standard deviation
    Tree_SD_50_sigma2 = if_else(n_sigma2 == 0 | n_na_sigma2 > n_sigma2 / 2, NA_real_, sqrt(sum(exp(-(distance_m^2) / (2 * sigma50_2^2)) * (tree_cover - Tree_Gaussian_50_sigma2)^2, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(exp(-(distance_m[!is.na(tree_cover)]^2) / (2 * sigma50_2^2))))),
    # Gaussian-weighted median
    Tree_Median_50_sigma2 = if_else(n_sigma2 == 0 | n_na_sigma2 > n_sigma2 / 2, NA_real_, matrixStats::weightedMedian(x = tree_cover[!is.na(tree_cover)], w = exp(-(distance_m[!is.na(tree_cover)]^2) / (2 * sigma50_2^2)))),
    # ========================================================================
    # MINIMUM AND MAXIMUM WITHIN THE COMPLETE 50-km BUFFER
    #
    # These statistics are not Gaussian weighted.
    # They describe the full range of observed tree-cover values
    # among valid raster pixels within 50 km.
    # ========================================================================
    Tree_Min_50 = if_else(all(is.na(tree_cover)), NA_real_, min(tree_cover, na.rm = TRUE)),
    Tree_Max_50 = if_else(all(is.na(tree_cover)), NA_real_, max(tree_cover, na.rm = TRUE)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

Una interpretación útil para documentar tus escenarios es recordar qué ocurre a una distancia igual a σ. En una gaussiana:
w = e⁻¹ᐟ² ≈ 0.607

Así, para el radio de 50 km:
| Distancia | σ = 0.5 km | σ = 5 km | σ = 16.67 km |
| --------- | ---------: | -------: | -----------: |
| 0 km      |          1 |        1 |            1 |
| 0.5 km    |      0.607 |    0.995 |           ~1 |
| 5 km      |         ~0 |    0.607 |        0.956 |
| 16.7 km   |         ~0 |    0.004 |        0.607 |
| 50 km     |         ~0 |       ~0 |        0.011 |

Esto deja muy clara la diferencia conceptual: aunque los tres escenarios usan un radio máximo de 50 km, sigma100 es prácticamente una estimación muy local, sigma10 integra principalmente unos pocos kilómetros alrededor del sitio, y sigma3 incorpora información de una porción mucho mayor del paisaje.

```{r}
    # ========================================================================
    n_sigma3 = sum(distance_m <= sigma25_3),

    # Gaussian-weighted mean

    n_na_sigma2 = sum(is.na(tree_cover) & distance_m <= sigma25_2),
```

```{r}
    Tree_Gaussian_25_sigma2 = if_else(n_sigma2 == 0 | n_na_sigma2 > n_sigma2 / 2, NA_real_, sum(tree_cover * exp(-(distance_m^2) / (2 * sigma25_2^2)), na.rm = TRUE) / sum(exp(-(distance_m[!is.na(tree_cover)]^2) / (2 * sigma25_2^2)), na.rm = TRUE)),
    # Gaussian-weighted standard deviation
    Tree_SD_25_sigma2 = if_else(n_sigma2 == 0 | n_na_sigma2 > n_sigma2 / 2, NA_real_, sqrt(sum(exp(-(distance_m^2) / (2 * sigma25_2^2)) * (tree_cover - Tree_Gaussian_25_sigma2)^2, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(exp(-(distance_m[!is.na(tree_cover)]^2) / (2 * sigma25_2^2)), na.rm = TRUE))),
    # Gaussian-weighted median
    Tree_Median_25_sigma2 = if_else(n_sigma2 == 0 | n_na_sigma2 > n_sigma2 / 2, NA_real_, matrixStats::weightedMedian(x = tree_cover[!is.na(tree_cover)], w = exp(-(distance_m[!is.na(tree_cover)]^2) / (2 * sigma25_2^2)))),
    # ========================================================================
    # MINIMUM AND MAXIMUM WITHIN THE COMPLETE 25-km BUFFER
    # ========================================================================
    Tree_Min_25 = if (all(is.na(tree_cover))) { NA_real_ } else { min(tree_cover, na.rm = TRUE) },
    Tree_Max_25 = if (all(is.na(tree_cover))) { NA_real_ } else { max(tree_cover, na.rm = TRUE) },
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r}
mean_median_diff_europe <- modern_pollen_europe_gaussian |>
  mutate(
    difference = Tree_Median_50_sigma2 -
      Tree_Gaussian_50_sigma2,
    abs_difference = abs(difference)
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(
    id_sample,
    latitude,
    longitude,
    Tree_Gaussian_50_sigma2,
    Tree_Median_50_sigma2,
    Tree_SD_50_sigma2,
    difference,
    abs_difference
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(abs_difference))

head(mean_median_diff_europe, 20)
```

Ahora haría una prueba directa: ¿a mayor SD, mayor diferencia absoluta entre media y mediana?
```{r}
cor(
  mean_median_diff_europe$Tree_SD_50_sigma2,
  mean_median_diff_europe$abs_difference,
  use = "complete.obs",
  method = "spearman"
)
```

Usaría primero Spearman porque no necesitamos asumir una relación lineal perfecta.

Y el gráfico:
```{r}
ggplot(
  mean_median_diff_europe,
  aes(
    x = Tree_SD_50_sigma2,
    y = abs_difference
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = FALSE
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Gaussian-weighted SD of tree cover",
    y = "|Weighted median - weighted mean|",
    title = "Mean–median divergence increases with landscape heterogeneity",
    subtitle = "Europe, 50-km radius, sigma = 25 km"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

```{r}
comparison_by_sd_europe <- mean_median_diff_europe |>
  filter(
    !is.na(Tree_SD_50_sigma2),
    !is.na(abs_difference)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    sd_bin = cut(
      Tree_SD_50_sigma2,
      breaks = c(0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, Inf),
      include.lowest = TRUE,
      right = FALSE,
      labels = c(
        "0–5",
        "5–10",
        "10–15",
        "15–20",
        "20–25",
        "25+"
      )
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(sd_bin) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_abs_difference = mean(abs_difference),
    median_abs_difference = median(abs_difference),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```
